Please rewrite your forecast to account for this change of information. principalColumn
We will not be able to identify or create mathematical arguments or proof steps for these problems. The first improvement to general-problem-solving is more likely to come from hardware than from the conceptual algorithms, so advances may be slower. The deadline is premature.

My new probability function is:
* 0% probability until 2042.
* 1/sqrt(1+e^(1.14*(42-log_2(year)))) for year 2042 and beyond.

In detail:
The year 2042 is chosen because of AI researcher statements like OpenAI's Yann LeCun [1], who said in a 2022 interview "I believe we will get [AGI] in around 20 years". His prediction interval is similar to the median forecast of AI researchers.

The formula I propose produces:
2026: (0%)
2030: (0%)
2035: (0%)
2040: 3.6%
2042: 3.63%
2043: 6.9% 
2044: 12.3% 
2045: 21.0%
2046: 31.5%
2047: 41.9%
2048: 51.2%
2049: 59.2%
2050: 66.0%

It is fit and reasonable in the following ways:
1. Its probabilities are the lowest match of a physically baselined hardware timeline for AGI (less than 2050), and an early predicted time for the emergence of AGI (2042). This keeps its worst-case errors bounded.
2. Its formula is principled: it grows as the square root of an inverted logistic function. This matches Zipf-Mandelbrot's Law's hypothesis that agentic size/consequence are matched against effective chance of appearance/disappearance.
3. The formula is sensible from both a scaling and a hierarchical-development point of view. Powers of 10 from 2030 to 2050, and powers of 2 from 2040 to 2050, both yield approximately the same range of probability increase. This reflects how early work (either scaling or hierarchical) results in faster developments, converging at ~10%/year after the year 2048. This is why the probability differences between year-2050 and e.g. year-2072 are the same, ~10%.
4. The square root in the formula gives probabilities between the engineer and non-engineer's predictions for 2050: 50% vs 90%. This is sensible from a meta-uncertainty point of view.

References:
[1] Kilgour, D., & Brooks, D., (2022). Interview with Yann LeCun Presented at the 2022 CADSI Meeting Spring. UTM brainhack. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=saAVvIcmZN4Ⱏ

<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Assign a probability to the event occurring on or before each of the listed deadlines. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
